Interpretation:
 INTERPRETATION(S):
   The APTIMA Combo 2 Assay detects the presence or absence of Neisseria
 gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis ribosomal RNA in female cervical and
 vaginal swabs, male urethral swabs, and female/male urine specimens. The
 assay uses a target amplification nucleic acid probe technology and is  run on
 the TIGRIS DTS Automated Analyzer. Data on the performance of nucleic acid
 testing (NAATs) for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhea in patients
 under 16 is limited. This assay has not specifically been evaluated for
 patients under 16. Consultation with an expert is recommended before the
 performance and interpretation of NAAT in this context, to minimize the
 possibility of false positive and false negative results. This assay is not
 intended for the evaluation of suspected sexual abuse or for other
 medico-legal indications.

 INTERPRETATION(S): All persons below our lower limit of 7 are considered "Deficient".
 
 Values greater than the upper limit of our reference range are considered
 "Normal" in accordance with guidance from the Tietz Textbook on Clinical
 Chemistry, which states that values greater than the upper limit of the
 reference range are encountered in any condition associated with younger than
 normal RBC's (as in hemolytic anemias not due to G6PD deficiency), but are of
 no clinical significance.
 
 Specimen: 3-5 mL whole blood (EDTA tube,Lavender top - do not use twist-off
 caps).  Do not freeze G6PD samples.  Refrigerated samples are good for only 7
 days; ship ASAP after collection.  Excessive leukocytes or platelets, which
 are high in G6PD, may interfere in the assay.  Reticulocytes have higher G6PD

 severe hemolytic crisis.

Discussed hallux abductovalgus, lower extremity biomechanics, and treatment options.
Non-Surgical Treatment
Sometimes observation of the bunion is    all that's needed. To reduce the chance of damage to the joint, periodic evaluation and x-
rays is    advised.
In many other cases, however, some type of treatment is    needed. Early treatments are aimed at easing the pain of bunions, but they 
won't reverse the deformity itself. These include:
•Changes in    shoewear. Wearing the right kind of shoes is    very important. Choose shoes that have a   wide toe box and 
forgo those with pointed toes or high heels which may aggravate the condition. 
•Padding. Pads placed over the area of the bunion can help minimize pain. 
•Activity modifications. Avoid activity that causes bunion pain. 
•Medications. Oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, may be recommended to reduce pain and inflammation. 
•Icing. Applying an ice pack helps reduce inflammation and pain. 
•Injection therapy. Although rarely used in    bunion treatment, injections of corticosteroids may be useful in treating the 
inflamed bursa (fluid-filled sac located around a joint) sometimes seen with bunions. 
•Orthotic devices. Custom orthotic devices (arch supports) may be provided. 
Surgery
If   non-surgical treatments fail to relieve bunion pain and when the pain of a   bunion interferes with daily activities, surgery may be 
considered. 
A   variety of surgical procedures are available to treat bunions. The procedures are designed to remove the "bump" of bone, correct 
the changes in    the bony structure of the foot, and correct soft tissue changes that may also have occurred. The goal of surgery is 
the reduction of pain.
In selecting the procedure or combination of procedures for any particular case, the extent of deformity based on the x-ray findings, 
age, activity level, and other factors are taken into consideration. The length of the recovery period will vary, depending on the 
procedure or procedures performed.
-  recommend temporary profile: no running; avoid high impact activity; stand/walk/climb stairs at own pace and distance

Note Written by CAPRA,JASON @ 25 Aug 2015 1010 CDT
Transforaminal epidural steroid Injection, right L5-S1
Interventionalist: Dr. Capra
Tuesday, August 25, 2015
History: The patient suffers from chronic back pain with radicular symptoms. Clinical examination and 
history suggests that the administration of epidural steroids may help relieve this pain. 
Informed consent was obtained from the patient regarding risks and complications. The risks, benefits, 
and alternatives of an epidural steroid injection were discussed with the patient. Transient exacerbation of 
pain, possible leg weakness, post dural puncture headache, and warning signs for epidural 
hematoma/abscess were also discussed. The patient elected to proceed after all questions were 
answered. The patient was taken to a   procedure room and was placed in    prone position. Vital signs were 
taken. The lumbosacral region was prepped and draped in    a   sterile manner. A time out was preformed 
prior to the procedure. The interventionalist wore sterile gloves, a   mask, and a   hat.
A    25  Ga 3.5  inch spinal  needle was used for the procedure.  Fluoroscopic guidance was  used to guide 
the needle. The needle was advanced from an oblique position  and aimed under the 6  oclock 
position of  the appropriate pedicle.  In the  AP  projection the needle was  angled upward  under 
the appropriate transverse process to place it   in    close proximity to the nerve root to be blocked. 
The needle was not allowed to travel farther medial than the medial pedicular border to ensure 
that there was no possibility of dural puncture.  AP, oblique and lateral fluoroscopic images were 
used for  precise needle  positioning  within the  neuroforamen. If the  patient  experienced a 
paresthesia during needle placement the  needle was immediately retracted to  prevent post-
procedure nerve irritation.  Once  needle  placement was confirmed to be extravascular  and 
extradural with the injection of 1mL omnipaque 200, the patient received 8mg Decadron and 1ml 
of .5% Bupivacaine after careful aspiration for blood and CSF.

Non-Surgical Treatment
Sometimes observation of the bunion is    all that's needed. To reduce the chance
of damage to the joint, periodic evaluation and x-rays is    advised.
In many other cases, however, some type of treatment is    needed. Early
treatments are aimed at easing the pain of bunions, but they won't reverse
the deformity itself. These include:
?Changes in    shoewear. Wearing the right kind of shoes is    very important.
Choose shoes that have a wide toe box and forgo those with pointed toes or
high heels which may aggravate the condition.
?Padding. Pads placed over the area of the bunion can help minimize pain.

?Activity modifications. Avoid activity that causes bunion pain.
?Medications. Oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, may be recommended
to reduce pain and inflammation.
?Icing. Applying an ice pack helps reduce inflammation and pain.
?Injection therapy. Although rarely used in    bunion treatment, injections of
corticosteroids may be useful in    treating the inflamed bursa (fluid-filled
sac located around a joint) sometimes seen with bunions.
?Orthotic devices. Custom orthotic devices (arch supports) may be provided.
Surgery
If   non-surgical treatments fail to relieve bunion pain and when the pain of a
bunion interferes with daily activities, surgery may be considered.
A   variety of surgical procedures are available to treat bunions. The
procedures are designed to remove the "bump" of bone, correct the changes in
the bony structure of the foot, and correct soft tissue changes that may also
have occurred. The goal of surgery is    the reduction of pain.
In selecting the procedure or combination of procedures for any particular
case, the extent of deformity based on the x-ray findings, age, activity
level, and other factors are taken into consideration. The length of the
recovery period will vary, depending on the procedure or procedures
performed.

Note Written by CAPRA,JASON @ 25 Aug 2015 1010 CDT
Transforaminal epidural steroid Injection, right L5-S1
Interventionalist: Dr. Capra
Tuesday, August 25, 2015
History: The patient suffers from chronic back pain with radicular symptoms.
Clinical examination and history suggests that the administration of epidural
steroids may help relieve this pain.
Informed consent was obtained from the patient regarding risks and
complications. The risks, benefits, and alternatives of an epidural steroid
injection were discussed with the patient. Transient exacerbation of pain,
possible leg weakness, post dural puncture headache, and warning signs for
epidural hematoma/abscess were also discussed. The patient elected to proceed
after all questions were answered. The patient was taken to a   procedure room
and was placed in prone position. Vital signs were taken. The lumbosacral
region was prepped and draped in    a   sterile manner. A   time out was preformed
prior to the procedure. The interventionalist wore sterile gloves, a   mask,
and a   hat.
A   25 Ga 3.5 inch spinal needle was used for the procedure.  Fluoroscopic
guidance was used to guide the needle. The needle was advanced from an
oblique position and aimed under the 6   oclock position of the appropriate
pedicle.  In the AP projection the needle was angled upward under the
appropriate transverse process to place it   in    close proximity to the nerve
root to be blocked. The needle was not allowed to travel farther medial than
the medial pedicular border to ensure that there was no possibility of dural
puncture.  AP, oblique and lateral fluoroscopic images were used for precise
needle positioning within the neuroforamen. If   the patient experienced a
paresthesia during needle placement the needle was immediately retracted to
prevent post-procedure nerve irritation.  Once needle placement was confirmed
to be extravascular and extradural with the injection of 1mL omnipaque 200,
the patient received 8mg Decadron and 1ml of .5% Bupivacaine after careful
aspiration for blood and CSF.
The patient experienced a very mild but concordant radicular pressure during
injection of the treatment solution, which further confirmed needle placement
to the affected nerve root.
Sedation:
Complications: None
Post procedure pain score: 3/10
 The patient was released from the procedure room after confirming that vital
signs were stable. The patient was given instructions to proceed to the ED
immediately if   new onset leg weakness, saddle anesthesia, bowel incontinence,
bladder incontinence, prolonged bleeding, severe back pain, or any other
concerning side effects were noted. The patient will call the pain clinic to
schedule a   post procedure follow up visit.

is    greatly improved after his surgeries, but it   has flared up today and he
